summary:
Environmental changes happen gradually, making them difficult to notice until serious damage occurs. Rising sea temperatures, changing wind patterns, and increasing sea levels threaten coastal areas, while declining soil moisture and changing rainfall patterns put farms, forests, and water resources at risk. By the time these problems become visible, recovery can be expensive. Governments need a way to identify these changes early, understand where they are happening, and prepare before the damage becomes severe.

Solution

CASTD is an environmental monitoring application with two sections: Coastal Watch and Soil Watch. Using historical NASA and other trusted environmental datasets, it helps users monitor changes in ocean and soil conditions. Users can select locations, choose environmental variables, and analyze long-term trends. The application removes seasonal variations and uses three statistical tests with a 95% confidence threshold to identify significant changes. It compares multiple locations, ranks areas based on their environmental trends, investigates possible contributing factors, and provides statistical projections for 2030, 2050, and 2100 with uncertainty ranges. Finally, CASTD turns its findings into simple alerts and precautionary recommendations, helping governments prepare for environmental risks rather than reacting after damage has occurred.
details:
What it does and how it works
CASTD (Coastal Area and Soil Trend Detection) is a web app that spots slow, harmful changes in the sea and the soil before they become serious. It offers two separate paths. One helps you judge the risk of a coastal area. The other helps you find soil that is gradually drying out.

You pick one or more places on a map, choose what to measure, and press run. The app gathers NASA data for each place and takes out the normal seasonal ups and downs. It then checks whether what remains is a real long-term trend or just chance, using three statistical tests and a 95 percent confidence level. You see what is changing, how quickly per decade, and whether the change is significant.

When you choose several places, the app ranks them from most to least severe. For each result it suggests possible causes and shows each cause’s own trend. It also draws a straight-line outlook to 2030, 2050 and 2100 with a likely range, and ends with an alert, a verdict and precaution policy. The soil path adds a farm calendar, and the coastal path adds a sea calendar with swimming ratings.

Benefits

  • Planners and governments can see where harm is building before it becomes expensive to fix.
  • One simple method covers two problems, with results in plain words and no expert knowledge needed.
  • The ranking shows where to act first.
  • It works in any web browser with nothing to install.

Intended impact
Changes in the sea and soil build up over decades, so there is time to prepare. We want governments to make long-term plans and early prevention policy today. That includes protecting coasts and beaches, planning for drought and water supply, and deciding where to restore forests and plant tree belts on drying land. Later, we plan to add NASA vegetation and forest-loss data to confirm where forest is missing.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: Python for the server and statistics, and JavaScript, HTML and CSS for the web page.
  • Data: NASA POWER (MERRA-2 model) for soil wetness, sea surface temperature (a model value), wind, air temperature, rain, clouds and sunlight.
  • Optional sea data: PSMSL tide gauges for sea level, and Open-Meteo Marine for wave height and period.
  • Other tools: the Python requests library, Leaflet and OpenStreetMap for the map, GitHub to store the code, and Render to host the app.
  • Testing and help: we ran automated browser tests (Playwright) on simulated data, and used the AI assistant Claude to help write and test the code and documents.
  • Hardware: none, since it runs in a browser.

What makes it creative

  • A single app and method handle two very different problems, kept in separate sections to avoid confusion.
  • It turns difficult statistics into plain answers about what changed, where, by how much, and whether it is real.
  • Each possible cause shows its own trend, and the verdict says whether that trend is harmful.
  • It does not stop at charts; it finishes with precaution policy people can act on.

What we considered

  • Honesty: the outlook is a straight line from past trends, not a forecast, and causes are evidence, not proof.
  • Data limits: results describe a region of about 25 to 50 kilometres, not a single beach or field. NASA’s sea temperature is a model value, so its trend may look steeper than satellite records.
  • Untested sources: sea level, wave height and wave period come from non-NASA sources that we have not tested live.
  • Safety: alerts are rough guides, not official warnings, and people should follow lifeguards, flags and local authorities.
  • Ease of use: plain words, two colour-coded sections, and no login or token.
  • Fair comparison: every place is ranked using the same method, so comparisons are consistent.
